'''assuagement''' (a-swāj′ment), ''n.'' [< OF. ''asuagement'', < ''asuager'': see ''assuage'' and ''-ment''.] '''1.''' The act of assuaging; mitigation; abatement. ''Spenser''.—'''2.''' An alleviative; a sedative.

'''assuager''' (a-swā′jėr), ''n.'' One who assuages or allays; that which mitigates or abates.

'''assuasive''' (a-swā′siv), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ''as-''<sup>1</sup> + ''suasive'', as in ''persuasive'', with reference to ''assuage''.] '''I.''' ''a.'' Softening; mitigating; tranquilizing; soothing. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Music her soft ''assuasive'' voice applies.
{{right|''Pope'', St. Cecilia’s Day, l. 25.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' A soothing medicine or application.

'''assubjugate†''' (a-sub′jö-gāt), ''v. t.'' [< ''as-''<sup>1</sup> + ''subjugate''.] To reduce to subjugation; put into a low or unworthy position; debase. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>No, this thrice worthy and right valiant lord
Must not . . . ''assubjugate'' his merit . . .
By going to Achilles.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., ii. 3.}}}}

'''assuefaction†''' (as-wē-fak′shọn), ''n.'' [< L. as if *''assuefactio(n-)'', < ''assuefacere'', pp. ''assuefactus'', make accustomed to, habituate, < ''assuetus'', pp. of ''assuescere'', accustom (see ''assuete''), + ''facere'', make.] The act of accustoming; the state of being accustomed; use; habituation.
{{smaller block|Right and left, as part inservient unto the motive faculty, are differenced by degrees, by use, and ''assuefaction''.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Vulg. Err., iv. 6.}}}}

'''assuete†''', ''a.'' [< L. ''assuetus'', pp. of ''assuescere'', accustom, habituate, < ''ad'', to, + ''suescere'', inceptive of *''suere'', be wont: see ''custom''.] Accus-

'''assumptious''' (a̤-sump′shus), ''a.'' [< ''assumption'' + ''-ous.'' Cf. ''presumptuous.''] Assuming; presumptuous. [Rare.]

'''assumptive''' (a̤-sump′tiv), ''a.'' [< L. ''assumptivus'', taken in addition, < ''assumptus'', pp. of ''assumere'', take, assume: see ''assume.''] '''1.''' Capable of being assumed; assumed.
{{smaller block|Writing under an ''assumptive'' character.
{{right|''Wycherly'', Plain Dealer, Pref.}}}}
'''2.''' Marked or characterized by assumptions.
{{smaller block|Trivial, scholastic, and ''assumptive'' methods.
{{right|''G. S. Hall'', German Culture, p. 312.}}}}
{{smaller block|'''Assumptive arms''', in ''her.'': (''a'') Formerly, arms not paternal, assumed in consequence of an exploit. (''b'') Now, arms which a person has a right, with the approbation of his sovereign and of the heralds, to assume. (''c'') Armorial bearings improperly assumed. [Rare in last use.] Also called ''arms of assumption.''}}

'''assumptively''' (a̤-sump′tiv-li), ''adv.'' In an assumptive or assumed manner; by way of assumption.

'''assurable''' (a̤-shör′a̤-bl), ''a.'' [< ''assure'' + ''-able.''] Capable of being assured; suitable for insurance: as, an ''assurable'' property.

'''assurance''' (a̤-shör′ans), ''n.'' [< ME. ''assuraunce'', < OF. ''asseürance'', F. ''assurance'' = Sp. ''aseguranza'' = It. ''assecuranza'' (= E. ''assecurance'', q. v.), < ML. ''assecurantia'', < ''assecurare'', assure: see ''assure'' and ''-ance.''] '''1.''' The act of assuring; a formal or earnest statement intended to produce belief or conviction; a positive declaration intended to give confidence: as, I trusted to his ''assurances.''

'''ass’s-foot''' (ȧs′ez-fu̇t), ''n.'' Same as ''coltsfoot.''

'''assuade''' (a̤-swād′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''assuaded'', ppr. ''assuading''.   [< L. ''as-'' for ''ad-'' + ''suadere'', advise: see ''suasion'', and cf. ''persuade''.]   To present as advice; urge persuasively.   ''N. E. D.''

'''assuage''' (a̤-swāj′), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''assuaged'', ppr. ''assuaging''.   [Early mod. E. also ''asswage'', ''aswage'', and by apheresis ''swage''; < ME. ''asuagen'', ''aswagen'', < OF. ''asouager'', ''asuager'', ''asoager'' = Pr. ''assuaviar'', ''asuaviar'', < ML. as if *''assuaviare'', < L. ''ad'', to, + ''suavis'', sweet: see ''suave'' and ''sweet''. Cf. ''abridge'', < L. ''abbreviare''; ''allege''<sup>2</sup>, < LL. ''alleviare'', etc.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' To soften, in a figurative sense; allay; mitigate, ease, or lessen, as pain or grief; moderate; appease or pacify, as passion or tumult.
{{smaller block|<poem>Yet he with strong perswasions her ''asswaged'',
And wonne her will to suffer him depart.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. vi. 43.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Refreshing winds the summer’s heats ''assuage''.</poem>
{{right|''Addison.''}}}}
{{smaller block|For the first time in history, she [the church] inspired thousands to devote their entire lives, through sacrifice and danger, to the single object of ''assuaging'' the sufferings of humanity. {{right|''Welsh'', Eng. Lit., I. 81.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn.''' ''Alleviate'', ''Relieve'', ''Mitigate'', etc. (see ''alleviate''); to appease, mollify, temper (see lists under ''alleviate'' and ''allay''<sup>1</sup>).}}

'''II.†''' ''intrans.'' To abate or subside; grow less: as, “let thin hert ''assuage'',” ''Gower''; “the waters ''asswaged'',” Gen. viii. 1.

'''assuagement''' (a-swāj′ment), ''n.''   [< OF. ''asuagement'', < ''asuager'': see ''assuage'' and ''-ment''.]   '''1.''' The act of assuaging; mitigation; abatement.   ''Spenser''.—'''2.''' An alleviative; a sedative.

'''assuager''' (a-swā′jėr), ''n.'' One who assuages or allays; that which mitigates or abates.

'''assuasive''' (a-swā′siv), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< ''as-''<sup>1</sup> + ''suasive'', as in ''persuasive'', with reference to ''assuage''.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' Softening; mitigating; tranquilizing; soothing. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Music her soft ''assuasive'' voice applies.
{{right|''Pope'', St. Cecilia’s Day, l. 25.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' A soothing medicine or application.

'''assubjugate†''' (a-sub′jö-gāt), ''v. t.''   [< ''as-''<sup>1</sup> + ''subjugate''.]   To reduce to subjugation; put into a low or unworthy position; debase. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>No, this thrice worthy and right valiant lord
Must not . . . ''assubjugate'' his merit . . .
By going to Achilles.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., ii. 3.}}}}

'''assuefaction†''' (as-wē-fak′shọn), ''n.''   [< L. as if *''assuefactio(n-)'', < ''assuefacere'', pp. ''assuefactus'', make accustomed to, habituate, < ''assuetus'', pp. of ''assuescere'', accustom (see ''assuete''), + ''facere'', make.]   The act of accustoming; the state of being accustomed; use; habituation.
{{smaller block|Right and left, as part inservient unto the motive faculty, are differenced by degrees, by use, and ''assuefaction''.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Vulg. Err., iv. 6.}}}}

'''assuete†''', ''a.''   [< L. ''assuetus'', pp. of ''assuescere'', accustom, habituate, < ''ad'', to, + ''suescere'', inceptive of *''suere'', be wont: see ''custom''.]   Accustomed; practised.   ''Blount.''

'''assuetude†''' (as′wẹ̄-tūd), ''n.''   [< L. ''assuetudo'', custom, < ''assuetus'', pp.: see ''assuete''. Cf. ''desuetude''.]   Custom; habit; habitual use.
{{smaller block|''Assuetude'' of things hurtful doth make them lose their force to hurt.
{{right|''Bacon'', Nat. Hist., § 67.}}}}

'''assumable''' (a̤-sū′ma̤-bl), ''a.''   [< ''assume'' + ''-able''.]   Capable of being assumed or taken for granted.

'''assumably''' (a̤-sū′ma̤-bli), ''adv.'' As may be assumed; presumably.
{{smaller block|The Macfarlane Highlanders, who were armed ''assumably'' with target and broadsword.
{{right|''N. and Q.'', 6th ser., XII. 40.}}}}

'''assume''' (a̤-sūm′), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''assumed'', ppr. ''assuming''.   [< L. ''assumere'', take to one’s self, take up, receive, accept, claim, assume, < ''ad'', to, + ''sūmere'', take, contr. from *''subimere'', < ''sub'', under, + ''emere'', take, buy: see ''emption'', ''emptor'', ''redeem''.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To take into relation or association; adopt; take in; admit: as, “Enoch and Elias were ''assumed'' up into heaven,” ''Abp. Abbot.'' See ''assumption'', 5. [Archaic.]
{{smaller block|The sixth was a young knight . . . ''assumed'' into that honourable company.
{{right|''Scott.''}}}}
'''2.''' To take upon one’s self; undertake: as, to ''assume'' the responsibility of a proceeding; to ''assume'' office; to ''assume'' an obligation.
{{smaller block|''Assume'' thy wingèd throne, thou Vesper of our throng!
{{right|''Shelley'', Adonais, st. 46.}}}}
{{smaller block|Among those subject kings whom the Assyrians had established in Egypt the descendants of the first Necho ''assumed'', after the fall of Nineveh, the position of independent sovereigns.
{{right|''Von Ranke'', Univ. Hist. (trans.), p. 83.}}}}

'''3.''' To take or put on one’s self; invest one’s self with: as, to ''assume'' the garb of a mendicant, or the figure of an animal; to ''assume'' a severe aspect; “to ''assume'' man’s nature,” ''Milton'', P. L., iii. 303.
{{smaller block|They say the devil can ''assume'' heaven’s brightness,
And so appear to tempt us.
{{right|''Fletcher'', Loyal Subject, iii. 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|Caroline . . . had persuaded Mrs. Pryor to ''assume'' her bonnet and summer shawl, and to take a walk with her.
{{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Shirley, xxi.}}}}
{{smaller block|Society never ''assumed'' the military type in England which it ''assumed'' upon the continent.
{{right|''J. Fiske'', Amer. Pol. Ideas, p. 123.}}}}
{{smaller block|Wheat quickly ''assumes'' new habits of life.
{{right|''Darwin'', Var. of Animals and Plants, p. 333.}}}}
'''4.''' To apply to one’s self; appropriate.
{{smaller block|His majesty might well ''assume'' the complaint of King David. {{right|''Clarendon.''}}}}
{{smaller block|His Holiness the Pope, by virtue of being Christ’s Vicegerent upon earth, piously ''assumed'' to himself a right to dispose of the territories of infidels as he thought fit.
{{right|''A. Hamilton'', Works, II. 68.}}}}
{{smaller block|Hastings had ceased to difference his arms as a cadet, and ''assumed'' them unbroken. {{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XI. 687.}}}}
'''5.''' To take for granted or without proof; suppose as a fact; postulate: as, to ''assume'' a principle in reasoning.
{{smaller block|Generally it may be ''assumed'' that rhetoric will not survive the age of the ceremonious in manners and the gorgeous in costume. {{right|''De Quincey'', Rhetoric.}}}}
{{smaller block|If the step from mechanics to chemistry is known, has been proved, and is admitted, that from chemistry to life is ''assumed'', and ''assumed'' without the slightest reason.
{{right|''Beale'', Protoplasm, p. 117.}}}} 6. To take fictitiously; pretend to possess; take in appearance: as, to ''assume'' the garb of humility.
{{smaller block|''Assume'' a virtue, if you have it not.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 4.}}}}
'''7†.''' To claim.
{{smaller block|Like a bold champion I ''assume'' the lists.
{{right|''Shak.'', Pericles, i. 1.}}}}
='''Syn. 6.''' To affect, feign, counterfeit.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To be arrogant; claim more than is due; presume.

'''assumedly''' (a̤-sū′med-li), ''adv.'' As is or may be assumed or taken for granted; presumably.

'''assument†''' (a̤-sū′ment), ''n.''   [< LL. ''assumentum'', a piece sewed on, < L. ''assuere'', sew on, < ''ad'', to, + ''suere'', sew, = E. ''sew'', q. v.]   A piece sewed on; a patch; an addition.
{{smaller block|The ''assument'' or addition Dr. Marshall never could find anywhere but in this Anglo-Saxonick translation.
{{right|''J. Lewis'', Hist. of Eng. Bibles, p. 9.}}}}

'''assumer''' (a̤-sū′mėr), ''n.'' One who assumes; an arrogant person.
{{smaller block|These high ''assumers'' and pretenders to reason.
{{right|''South.''}}}}
{{smaller block|To swear at the mention of ''assumers'' and pretenders to baronetcies.
{{right|''The Atlantic'', LII. 365.}}}}

'''assuming''' (a̤-sū′ming), ''p. a.'' Taking or disposed to take upon one’s self more than is just; disposed to attribute to one’s self undue importance; haughty; arrogant.
{{smaller block|<poem>His haughty looks and his ''assuming'' air
The son of Isis could no longer bear. ''Dryden.''</poem>}}
{{smaller block|A virtue that might repress the most ''assuming''.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', The Bee, No. 3.}}}} =Syn. Bold, forward, presuming, self-confident.

'''assuming†''' (a̤-sū′ming), ''n.'' Presumption.
{{smaller block|The vain ''assumings'' of some.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Poetaster.}}}}

'''assumingly''' (a̤-sū′ming-li), ''adv.'' In an assuming manner; arrogantly.

'''assumpsit''' (a-sump′sit), ''n.''   [L., he undertook; third pers. sing. perf. ind. of ''assumere'', assume, undertake: see ''assume.'']   In ''law:'' (''a'') An action lying for the recovery of damages sustained through the breach of a simple contract (that is, a promise not under seal), in which the plaintiff alleges that the defendant ''assumpsit'', that is, promised or undertook, to perform the act specified. {{smaller|In England and in most of the United States this, like the other common-law forms of action, has been superseded by statute.}} Hence—(''b'') An actionable promise, express or implied by law.

'''assumpt†''' (a-sumpt′), ''v. t.''   [< L. ''assumptus'', pp. of ''assumere'', take up: see ''assume.'']   '''1.''' To take up; raise. See ''assume, v. t.'', 1.
{{smaller block|She was ''assumpted'' into the cloud.
{{right|''Hall'', Hen. VIII., an. 14.}}}}
'''2.''' To assume, as a proposition or premise.
{{smaller block|Supposition ''assumpted'' is when a manifest supposition is ''assumpted'' to prove another thing withal, as . . . the disputer will ''assumpt'' this assertion, which saith that of false things there is no certain knowledge, and truth is not known but of true things. {{right|''Blundeville'', 1619.}}}}
'''3.''' To assume, as a property, attribute, etc.
{{smaller block|I do grant it to be Christ’s true body and flesh by a property of the nature ''assumpted'' to the Godhead; yea, and we do really eat and drink His flesh and blood after a certain real property.
{{right|''Ridley'', in R. W. Dixon’s Hist. Church of Eng., xvi., note.}}}}

'''4.''' To take to one’s self; put on; assume.

{{smaller block|And ''assumpted'', or tooke to his Arms . . . a Crosse Silver, in a field vert. {{right|''Bossewell'', Armorie, p. 22. (''N. E. D.'')}}}}

'''assumpt†''' (a̤-sumpt′), ''n.''   [< L. ''assumptum'', neut. of ''assumptus'', pp., assumed: see ''assumpt'', ''v.'']   That which is assumed; an assumption.

{{smaller block|The sum of all your ''assumpts''. {{right|''Chillingworth'', Relig. of Protestants, i. 1.}}}}

'''assumption''' (a̤-sump′shọn), ''n.''   [< ME. ''assumpcioun'', ''assumptioun'' (of the Virgin Mary), < ML. ''assumptio(n-)'', a taking up (into heaven); L., a taking up, adoption, the minor proposition of a syllogism; < ''assumere'', pp. ''assumptus'', take up, etc.: see ''assume''.]   '''1.''' The act of taking to one’s self; a taking upon one’s self; undertaking.

{{smaller block|Since the ''Assumption'' of our flesh, we know what shape to picture God in. {{right|''Selden'', Table-Talk, p. 55.}}}}
{{smaller block|An ''assumption'' of power not conferred by the Constitution and laws.
{{right|''D. Webster'', Speech, Senate, May 7, 1834.}}}}

'''2.''' The act of taking for granted, or supposing without proof; supposition.

{{smaller block|The ''assumption'' of a final cause in the structure of each part of animals and plants is as inevitable as the ''assumption'' of an efficient cause for every event. {{right|''Whewell'', Nov. Org. Renovatum, p. 105.}}}}

'''3.''' The thing supposed; a postulate or proposition assumed.

{{smaller block|Let well-weighed considerations, not stiff and peremptory ''assumptions'', guide thy discourses. {{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Christ. Mor., ii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|In fact, the putting of limits to human conception must always involve the ''assumption'' that our previous experience is universally valid in a theoretical sense; an ''assumption'' which we have already seen reason to reject. {{right|''W. K. Clifford'', Lectures, I. 155.}}}} '''4.''' In ''logic'', the minor premise in a categorical syllogism.
{{smaller block|Still more objectionable are the correlative terms proposition and ''assumption'' as synonymous for the major and minor premises.
{{right|''Sir W. Hamilton'', Logic.}}}}
{{smaller block|[This use of the word, originating with Cicero (Latin ''assumptio''), was revived in the sixteenth century, and is common in modern Latin, but is rare in English.]}}
'''5.''' The taking up of a person into heaven; specifically, the traditional anticipated resurrection or bodily taking up into heaven of the Virgin Mary after her death, celebrated by the Roman Catholic, Greek, and Oriental churches by the feast of the Assumption on the 15th of August.—'''6.''' Adoption, or making use of.
{{smaller block|It is evident that the prose psalms of our liturgy were chiefly consulted and copied by the perpetual ''assumptions'' of their words and combinations.
{{right|''T. Warton'', Hist. Eng. Poetry, III. 172.}}}}
'''7.''' In ''law'', the agreement of the transferee of property to pay obligations of the transferror which are chargeable on it.—'''8.''' A conceited disposition, characterized by a tendency to claim more than is one’s due; presumption.
{{smaller block|The priest, however arrogant his ''assumption'', makes a civil salute.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Prin. of Sociol., § 343.}}}}
{{smaller block|'''Arms of assumption.''' See ''arm''<sup>2</sup>, 7, and ''assumptive arms'', under ''assumptive''.—'''Assumption clause.''' See ''clause''.—'''Deed of assumption,''' in ''Scots law'', a deed executed by trustees under a trust deed or deed of settlement, assuming a new trustee or trustees. ='''Syn. 2''' and '''3.''' Conjecture, hypothesis, theory, postulate.—'''8.''' ''Pride, Presumption'', etc. (see ''arrogance''); officiousness, forwardness, self-confidence, self-conceit, face.}}

'''assumptious''' (a̤-sump′shus), ''a.''   [< ''assumption'' + ''-ous.'' Cf. ''presumptuous.'']   Assuming; presumptuous. [Rare.]

'''assumptive''' (a̤-sump′tiv), ''a.''   [< L. ''assumptivus'', taken in addition, < ''assumptus'', pp. of ''assumere'', take, assume: see ''assume.'']   '''1.''' Capable of being assumed; assumed.

''assecurantia'', < ''assecurare'', assure: see ''assure'' and ''-ance.'']   '''1.'''
